data.content_ref: inline:SRC_002's mechanism invokes the Law of Large Numbers, but a panel of non-experts all following the SAME explicit checklist is not applying independent judgments to independent samples — they are applying a shared deterministic procedure. The LLN averages out idiosyncratic stochastic noise across independent draws; here, any panel disagreement comes only from execution error in applying the same fixed protocol. If the checklist itself contains a systematic gap (which SRC_002 itself flags as a countercondition: 'The checklist contains a systemic error (shared bias)'), aggregation amplifies, not removes, the correlated error — the LLN does not apply. So the stated mechanism misidentifies the mathematical basis: the reliability gain (when it exists) comes from variance reduction in procedural execution and from the checklist encoding domain knowledge, NOT from the LLN 'averaging out' independent cognitive noise as claimed. The problem asks what evidence distinguishes genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance; SRC_002's LLN framing actively obscures that distinction because it treats all disagreement as independent noise rather than potentially-correlated compliance with a flawed protocol.
